blocks.title: Hugh Le Caine | Printed Circuit Keyboard (1962)
blocks.description: Hugh Le Caine's printed circuit keyboard is a pioneering development in the field of electronic interfaces, bring technology for printing circuit boards to the surface.

blocks.title: Printed Circuit Boards
blocks.description: Printed circuit boards (PCBs), first developed in 1936, enabled mass production of electronic designs, an advantage over wiring components by hand

blocks.title: Don Buchla | Music Easel (1973)
blocks.description: A more commercial but still extremely niche approach to keyboard interfaces to electronic music instruments came with Buchla's Music Easel, a concession to instrumentalists who wanted to a more standard way of playing his synthesizers. But unlike other keyboards, this interface allowed touch to influence any number of sonic parameters, not just the musical pitch.

blocks.title: CERN | Early capacitive touch screens at CERN
blocks.description: Elsewhere in the 1970s, CERN developed a touch-sensitive terminal that allowed for the control of procedures in particle accelerator experiments. Like touch sensitive keyboards, this also used copper traces to correlate changes in capacitance in the user's touch to areas of the screen

blocks.title: What IS an interface?
blocks.description: Using copper in these early touch interfaces, the human hand could engage with arbitarily complex systems, as long as that interaction could be reducible to binary operations (start/stop, on/off, etc.) or the gradations of a scalar value (e.g. volume level). This much follows the historical techno-centric definition of an interface. This reduction to binary operations has a parallel in the evolution of intelligent biology.

blocks.title: Max Bennett | A Brief History of Intelligence
blocks.description: Bennett's survey of intelligence in early life on earth makes a distinction between two types of symmetry: radial and bilateral. Compared to radial symmetry, bilateral symmetry allows complex navigation to emerge from a series of simple binary choices. Bilaterians now comprise nearly 100% of animal life on this planet.

blocks.title: What is it like to be a Roomba?
blocks.description: Bennett also draws a comparison to early versions of the Roomba, which did not construct models of its environment. Instead, like a bilaterian, it used proximity sensors to inform changes in direction. The term 'umwelt' describes the world perceived by a living organism, shaped by its cognitive and sensory capabilities. In this sense, the Roomba has its own umwelt, fit to its twin goals in life: to vacuum floors and to recharge when running low on battery.

blocks.title: Bilaterian navigation and the archetype of the labyrinth
blocks.description: Across many cultural traditions in history, this bilaterian mode of navigation is associated with the archetype of the labyrinth. The pioneering psychoanalyst Carl Jung conducted a comprehensive survey of labyrinths across across many civilizations, tracing its variations and valences but ultimately leading back to a common archetypal metaphor: that of human growth and individuation through the winding journey of the soul.

blocks.title: Chartres Cathedral (ca. 1200)
blocks.description: The Chartres Cathedral is a premiere example of this in medieval Europea, in which the labyrinth laid in tilework on the ground was meant to be literally traversed as a symbolic pilgrimage.

blocks.title: Terry Fox's Labyrinths
blocks.description: The artist Terry Fox focused a significant body of work on the labyrinth at the Chartres Cathedral in France. He translated the series of turns that make up the labyrinth into an experimental score for producing performances and sound art. One notable example of this is his audio mix of the purring of eleven cats according to this score.

blocks.title: Wacław Szpakowski, Rhythmical Lines (1900s-1940s)
blocks.description: Fox's unwindings of the labyrinth have a parallel to drawings made by the the Polish architect Wacław Szpakowski at the turn of the 20th century. Although he did not translate these into sounds directly, these lines are meant to be followed with the eyes as if walking an imaginary labyrinth and suggesting a kind of visual music. These more modern uses of the labyrinth that unlike for the roomba, navigation is simultaneously an inward and outward journey that is close to the heart of human experience.

blocks.title: Christopher Alexander's Fifteen Properties of Living Structures
blocks.description: In these examples, the meandering line represents movement, but lines also represent divisions. In this visual interpretation of Alexander's Fifteen Properties of Living Structures, the line of the labyrinth represents 'deep interlock' (also referred to as ambiguity, mututal embedding). Similar to 'connectedness', it shows two interlocking parts, but characterized by a level of inseparability. Deep interlock (or ambiguity, mututal embedding) as a living structure expresses the porousness of boundaries. Dyads can be simple to conceptualize as yin and yang, but their interpenetrations yield a rich confusion. Ornamentation ⊗ form, inside ⊗ outside, foreground ⊗ background, surface ⊗ interior, self ⊗ environment — these are all formulated as opposites, but each one also contains the other. Without clean boundaries, these pairings express tension more so than absolutes. A `clean` interface is a useful fiction at best.

blocks.title: Escaping Containment
blocks.description: What does all this mean for the roomba, what does it become when it leaves its intended environment? What is it really turning for? There's a much larger world outside the Roomba umwelt. Interfaces mediate exchanges between the self and environment. But how is environment determined? Given an interface, what is the world on the other side?

blocks.title: Human umwelt within the technologically mediated environment
blocks.description: The human umwelt is broader than the roomba, but like any organism, it is still subject to constraints. But an umwelt is not a fixed thing, it can be bound down by narrow interfaces, or expanded by wide ones, as we move through both physical and virtual environments.

blocks.title: Michel Redolfi | Sonic Waters at Bains de Bruxelles
blocks.description: Redolfi's concerts of Sonic Waters defamiliarize a particular environment: the indoor pool. He augments the space with both underwater and above-water speakers to create a sense of literally swimming in sound. Even without providing explicit scores or instructions, the modification of the environment influences the behavior of the audience, with sound acting as a soft interface to individual bodies.

blocks.title: Environments 1 | The Psychologically Ultimate Seashore (1969)
blocks.description: While sounds of various environments can now be found everywhere from cars to devices to aid sleep, Environments was the first mass market offering of such recordings. The very first recording, titled Psychologically Ultimate Seashore, was recorded at Coney Island and manipulated at Bell Labs. Unlike the literal immersion of Redolfi's Sonic Waters, this literal recording of ocean waves is also more portable, and demonstrates how a purely aural (and in this case simulated) environment can interface to the self.

blocks.title: Echolocation
blocks.description: Sound does have a direct relationship to environment, perhaps most clearly in the case of echolocation. While you can only see ahead of you, you can hear all around you. While we usually navigate by sound in this way, we do still share common neurobiological mechanisms with bats.

blocks.title: Sound and environment in the brainstem
blocks.description: Neurobiologically, spatial determination does not come directly from the ears, but from a region of the brainstem known as the Medial Superior Olive. Here, sounds from the two ears are combined and slight temporal differences are used to determine the spatial location of a sound.

blocks.title: Binaural beating: deep interlock of self and environment
blocks.description: Within the larger category of psychoacoustic phenomena (sound that you hear but don't objectively exist), binaural beating is particularly interesting for how it activates the Medial Superior Olive. Its original function, to detect spatial position, is fundamentally disoriented, and with that any meaningful distinction about where the sound 'comes from'. There is no meaningful distinction between foreground and background sound, or whether the sound is internal or external (deep interlock)
